6e66e188.title: 61 Seats: Israel Election, Netanyahu, Knesset #Shorts
6e66e188.summary: This Short broke out because people were searching for it. 46 of its 49 tracked views came from YouTube search, and none came from people scrolling the Shorts feed. It went up at 07:28 Israel time on 27 Oct 2026, about half an hour after polls opened in Israel's first election since Oct 7. The title stacked the words people were typing (Israel Election, Netanyahu, Knesset) next to '61 Seats', which became the headline number once exit polls showed neither bloc reaching it.
6e66e188.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 55 against a channel usual of about 5.5, so roughly 10x. The other 17 Shorts listed got 0 to 13 views. Only the long-titled Alaska megatsunami video (38) comes close.
- **Likes and comments:** 1 like and 0 comments, so about 1.8 likes per 100 views. The rest of the channel has 0 likes on every Short, so this is above the channel only by a single like. That is too small to count as a signal.
- **Traffic:** 46 of 49 Analytics views came from **YouTube search** (94%), 3 from the Shorts feed and 0 from outside YouTube. The breakout came almost entirely from search, not from the feed.
- **Retention:** The analytics row is 49 / 17.14 / 15, with no column labels. If 17.14 is minutes watched, the average view lasted about 21 seconds. If 15 is the average view duration, it was about 15 seconds. Either way, most viewers left well before the end. This is a guess based on how the API usually orders its columns.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** Countries are blank. We also don't know which search words people used, how often the video was shown in search, or how often those showings were clicked. At 55 views, one more good day could double the total. Treat this as a direction, not proof.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The script was not supplied, so this part is partly a guess. Searchers arrive already knowing what they want, so the hook matters less than matching their question. The opening number, '61', answers the question most searchers had: what does it take to win? With about 15–21 seconds watched on average, the most useful part has to land before second 15.

## Psychology
This was a curiosity gap on a deadline. On voting day nobody knows the result, and people look for a quick way to understand the race. The Short gave one threshold (61 of 120), one tension (neither bloc reaches it) and a next-steps plan (the president's pick, 28 + 14 days, or another election). That gives a sense of control over a confusing event. It did not get people to share or comment: 0 comments and no outside traffic. The video satisfied the searcher and they moved on.

## Topic and timing
Search results confirm that 27 Oct 2026 was election day for the 26th Knesset. It was the first vote since Oct 7, 2023, and the first in decades to come at the natural end of a term. CNN and Al Jazeera led their exit-poll and final-count coverage with the fact that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot could reach the 61 seats needed. The video's prediction turned out right, and its key number became the headline number. It was published at 10:58 IST (07:28 in Israel), just after polls opened, so it was in search before the big wave of interest. Search demand for Israel news is global and largely English-speaking, which fits the channel. Compare it with elections that got no lift. Lula wins Brazil got 6 views: it was a result, posted after the moment, against huge outlets. Surrey goes BC Conservative got 10, a local story. '14 Years in Power, Lost to a List With No Leader' got 5: it names no country and no person, so nobody can find it by search.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title is the clearest difference from every Short that didn't break out. It contains **three searchable proper nouns** (Israel Election, Netanyahu, Knesset) plus the deciding number. Most of the other Shorts have cryptic number-first titles ('289 Protests Began at One School', '2006 to Now: Jamia…') with nothing a person would type into search. The description repeats the key terms, gives the 120 seats and the 61 threshold, and has #IsraelElection, which helps search match the video. Its source list and note that the polls were not results probably did not affect views, but they protect trust. Shorts thumbnails hardly matter in search, so treat the thumbnail as neutral (a guess).

## Audience and algorithm
It reached people actively looking for this news, through search. The Shorts feed gave it only 3 views, so the feed did not pick it up. The weak retention probably explains why: the feed tests a video and rewards it if people watch to the end. Search rewards a relevant title that people click. The Alaska video (38 views, with a long descriptive title) probably reached viewers the same way, through search (a guess, since its traffic data wasn't given).

## What did not matter
- The AI hosts: they appear on every Short, including the ones that got 0 views.
- The #Shorts tag: it is on all of them.
- Publishing at a particular hour: Shorts at 00:32, 11:13 and 18:17 got few views, while this one won on event timing, not clock time.
- Elections as a category: Brazil, Canada and the unnamed '14 years' story all failed.
- Likes and comments: there weren't enough to drive anything.

## Repeat this
1. Pick scheduled world events with heavy English search demand.
2. Publish on the day, before the result, built around the one number that decides it.
3. Write titles as '[Number]: [Country] [Event], [Leader], [Institution]'.
4. Answer the searcher's question in the first 10 seconds.
5. Follow up within 24 hours with the result, using the same keywords.

## Test next
- Make a follow-up Short on the result ('No 61: Israel Election Result…') and see whether search sends viewers again.
- Publish a preview before the Japan rate decision with a keyword-heavy title, against a cryptic-title control.
- Put the payoff by second 10 and check whether the average view rises above 20 seconds and the Shorts feed starts to pick the video up.
- Run the same title format on an upcoming vote, such as the US, UK or EU, to see whether the lift was about Israel or about the format.

changes.rule: Each week, list the scheduled world events with big English-language search interest (national elections, central bank decisions, major launches or verdicts) and plan a Short that goes live on the day itself, before the result, explaining the one number that decides it.

Write every title as '[Decisive number]: [Country] [Event], [Main person], [Institution] #Shorts' with at least two proper nouns people would type into search, and never use a title made only of a number and a vague phrase.
Start the description with the exact search phrase people would use (for example 'Israel election 2026 explained: Knesset, Netanyahu, 61 seats') and add one hashtag naming the country and event.

Say the deciding number and what it means in the first sentence, and give the searcher's full answer (who needs what, and what happens next) by second 10, because most viewers leave around seconds 15–21.
Show the deciding number full-screen in the first frame with a simple threshold graphic (for example a 120-seat bar marked at 61) and keep it on screen until the answer is spoken.
When a scheduled-event Short gets more search traffic than usual, order a follow-up Short on the result within 24 hours with the same keywords plus 'Result' in the title.

6e66e188.owner: Pin this comment on the Israel Short: 'Update: final count is in. Neither bloc reached 61. Next: the president picks a candidate, who has 28 days (+14) to build a coalition, or Israel votes again. Full result Short coming next.' Then create a public playlist called 'Elections Explained' with the Israel, Brazil and BC Shorts and add every future election Short to it.
